beats.headline: Why does your code run 10x slower?
beats.subline: It isn't your algorithm. It's your memory layout fighting the CPU cache.
beats.narration: Your code is fast, but is it hardware-friendly? Modern CPUs don't fetch single bytes; they fetch 64-byte cache lines. If your data is scattered, you're wasting cycles waiting on DRAM.

beats.title: Cache-Friendly vs Cache-Hostile
beats.narration: LinkedLists force the CPU to chase pointers across the heap. Arrays keep data contiguous, allowing the hardware prefetcher to load your next values into L1 cache before you even ask for them.

beats.title: The 64-Byte Reality

steps.explanation: Contiguous memory guarantees the CPU fills the cache line efficiently.
Subsequent reads are L1 hits, costing ~1ns instead of ~100ns for DRAM.

beats.narration: When you read one int, the CPU grabs the whole 64-byte line. If your data is packed, you get 16 integers for the price of one memory fetch. That is mechanical sympathy.

beats.title: Latency Hierarchy
beats.narration: Missing L1 and hitting DRAM is a 100x penalty. Every time you traverse a linked structure, you risk stalling the CPU pipeline for hundreds of cycles.

beats.title: Part 1 Summary
takeaways: Arrays beat lists for cache locality
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): The hidden danger of False Sharing →
beats.narration: Stop chasing pointers. In Part 2, we tackle False Sharing—where two threads fighting over one cache line can destroy your throughput.

beats.headline: Why are your counters fighting?
beats.subline: Two threads, two variables, one cache line. The CPU is doing more work than you think.
beats.narration: You have two threads updating separate variables. They should be independent, right? Wrong. If they sit on the same cache line, the CPU forces them to serialize.

beats.title: The False Sharing Trap

steps.explanation: CPU coherence protocols (MESI) treat the whole line as one unit.
Writes invalidate the other core's cache, forcing a reload.

beats.narration: Because coherence works on 64-byte lines, updating the producer invalidates the consumer's cache line. They ping-pong ownership back and forth, stalling both cores.

beats.title: MESI Protocol Bottleneck
beats.narration: The CPU bus gets flooded with invalidation requests. This is the hidden cost of shared state in high-performance Java.

beats.title: Fixing with @Contended

steps.explanation: HotSpot inserts 128 bytes of padding around these fields.

beats.narration: The @Contended annotation forces the JVM to pad these fields onto different cache lines. No more contention, no more ping-ponging.

beats.title: Part 2 Summary

beats.narration: Padding is your best friend for concurrency. In Part 3, we dive into how branch predictors work—and how to write branchless code.

beats.headline: Is your IF statement costing you?
beats.subline: Modern CPUs guess your next move. If they guess wrong, you pay the price.
beats.narration: CPUs use deep pipelines to execute instructions. Branch predictors guess if an IF block will run. A wrong guess flushes the pipeline and costs 20 cycles.

beats.title: Branchy vs Branchless
beats.narration: Branchless code uses bitwise masks to simulate logic. It removes the jump entirely, keeping the pipeline full and execution time predictable.

beats.title: The Bitwise Mask

steps.explanation: Shifting 63 bits extracts the sign, creating a perfect filter.
C2 compiler often lowers this to a conditional move instruction.

beats.narration: This trick works because the CPU can perform arithmetic on masks faster than it can recover from a branch misprediction.

beats.title: Profiling Branches
beats.caption: Verify with perf stat
beats.narration: Don't guess. Use perf stat to see your miss rate. If it's high, it's time to optimize your logic.

beats.title: Part 3 Summary
takeaways: Use bitwise masks for random data

beats.narration: Branching is a gamble. In Part 4, we explore memory barriers and why your code behaves differently on ARM vs x86.

beats.headline: Why does your code fail on ARM?
beats.subline: x86 hides your concurrency bugs. ARM exposes them.
beats.narration: Your code works on Intel but crashes on Apple Silicon? That's the memory model. x86 is strong; ARM is weak. You need to understand barriers.

beats.title: x86 vs ARM Memory Models
beats.narration: x86 guarantees that stores become visible in order. ARM doesn't. Without explicit memory barriers, your threads will see stale data.

beats.title: VarHandle Release/Acquire

steps.explanation: Ensures all prior writes are visible before the sequence update.
Ensures subsequent reads happen after the sequence check.

beats.narration: VarHandle's release and acquire modes are the standard way to enforce happens-before edges without the full cost of a volatile write.

beats.title: Memory Barrier Types
beats.narration: These barriers tell the CPU to stop reordering. They are the foundation of lock-free concurrency in Java.

beats.title: Part 4 Summary
takeaways: x86 hides reordering; ARM exposes it
beats.narration: Memory models are tricky. Stick to JMM guarantees. In Part 5, we wrap up with the ultimate checklist for mechanical sympathy.

beats.headline: Ready to write hardware-aware Java?
beats.subline: From cache lines to memory barriers, you now have the blueprint.
beats.narration: You've gone from cache-hostile lists to hardware-aware memory models. You're ready to build the next generation of low-latency systems.

beats.title: High-Level vs Low-Latency
beats.narration: Don't optimize prematurely. Use standard Java for business logic, but use mechanical sympathy when you hit that microsecond wall.

beats.title: The Performance Checklist

steps.explanation: These four rules cover 90% of low-latency performance gains.

beats.narration: Follow this checklist. It's the difference between a system that stalls and a system that scales.
